  Running `git gc` there is the owner's call; run it when no window is mid-git.
- **Check `df -h /` before spawning clone-heavy agents, and when a git write fails with `Out of diskspace`.** Seat scratch (`~/.seat-tmp/<SEAT>/*_export`, clean clones, `ledger_sync` repos) and `/home/mandrake/rm/scratch` clones are 7-23 GB each and filled the root disk to 1.5 MB free. Delete finished ones at once (after 0 unpushed commits) and shallow- or `--filter=blob:none`-clone new ones.
- **A seat fanning out helpers must take pool clones (`scratch_clone.py`) or delete its own once landed.** 17 work-package clones under `~/rm/scratch/<SEAT>` made outside the pool were left after their work landed, read YOUNG to `scratch_reap` until the TTL, and fired a SCRATCH_OUTSIDE_CAP alarm for hours. A dirty ledger shard in such a clone is usually a rewritten copy of lines already on origin/main (check by set difference).
- **`scratch_reap` sanity END lines must count only what the run LEFT (rows not DELETED/YOUNG), never a whole-population count:** `session_dirs` and `rm_scratch_clones` each alarmed on live young work. Whole counts stay readings; `ops_watch` OP2 reads `rm_scratch_clones`.
- **Never clone or write large files under `/tmp`.** It is an 18G tmpfs shared by all workers, often 99-100% full, and its pages count against the seat's 10G `MemoryMax` (`src/RimMandrake/Utils/claude_bounded.sh`), staying counted after the writer dies: a 12G `git clone` into `/tmp` plus 16 parallel selftest workers (0.8-2.1G each) got the seat OOM-killed (23 processes). `git init` there fails 'Out of diskspace'. A mutant test that does `cp file /tmp/x.bak; mutate; cp /tmp/x.bak file` TRUNCATES the source (or writes a 64 KiB copy) when the first `cp` hits ENOSPC: take the backup with `git show HEAD:<path>` or on ext4 (`~/.seat-tmp/<seat>`) or `D:\ClaudeWork` scratch, `cmp` it before overwriting, and chain steps with `&&`. Seat processes use `TMPDIR=~/.seat-tmp/<SEAT>` so tests pass while anything writing `/tmp` directly fails; selftests also crashed ENOMEM with TMPDIR on `/mnt/d`, while `TMPDIR=~/.seat-tmp/<seat>/x` ran green. A full `/tmp` also shows as python scripts exiting 120 with EMPTY output (stdout flush ENOSPC), which looks like a silent tool failure: run `df /tmp` before trusting a silent exit 120. Delete any `/tmp` mutation-test scratch copies (~10 GB together once) when done; agent scratch never belongs in `/tmp`. Keep the selftest worker count low (`run_selftests.py --workers`).
- **A whole-repo export into tmpfs `/tmp` can be OOM-killed mid-stream by the 6 GiB tool cap** (tracked tree 3.58 GB; tar plus extract is about 7 GB), leaving a truncated tree that gives a confident wrong proof (a donor-off worker read flyers 5 and FAIL offline where the truth was 24 and PASS). Treat `tar: Unexpected EOF` or exit 137 in an export step as no result. Measured: `infrastructure/state/facts/oom_kills_2026-11-03.md`.
- **A full replay-tree write on `/mnt/d` (drvfs) is minutes versus seconds on ext4.** Exporting a 7.7 GB / 48k-file tree took ~20 min on drvfs vs 42 s on ext4 and `git add` >600 s vs 130 s; a full-tree checkout of this repo takes ~40 s on ext4 and outlasts 60 s on drvfs. Put scratch clones and exported trees on ext4 (e.g. `/home/mandrake/rm/<dir>`), never beside a log on `/mnt/d`. A tree export peaks ~4.4 GB RSS, so two at once sit near a 12G slice.

## Traps

Each of these cost at least one lost or mis-published change. Most are hook-enforced or fixed in the tools above; the
rest are discipline.

| trap | what happens | do instead |
|---|---|---|
| `git add a b c 2>/dev/null` | one missing path fails the WHOLE add silently; the commit then runs on an empty or partial index and "succeeds" | never silence `git add`; check `git show --stat HEAD` |
| a deleted path on `git add` | `git add <deleted>` errors and kills the `&&` chain; the push after it says "Everything up-to-date" | put a deleted path on the commit pathspec only |
| pathspec commit takes the WORKTREE | `git commit <path>` is an implicit `git add` of that path: a blob you staged with `update-index` is ignored, and a peer's unsaved lines in the same file ride along | check `git diff --stat <path>` first; build partial commits in a temp index (`GIT_INDEX_FILE`) |
| pathspec commit cannot remove-but-keep | `git rm --cached p` then `git commit p` re-adds `p` from the worktree | commit through a temp index (`GIT_INDEX_FILE=… git read-tree HEAD; git rm --cached …; write-tree; commit-tree`), then `git reset -q -- p` in the real index |
| untracked can't be pathspec-committed | `git commit <new file>` → "did not match any file(s) known to git"; a `git commit <dir>` silently skips new files in it | `git add -- <new file>` first (explicit path), then `git commit <paths>` |
| `-F -` after `--` | `git commit -- p -F -` treats `-F` and `-` as pathspecs | options before `--`, paths after |
| bare `git commit` | commits the WHOLE index, including what a helper staged in the same clone | always name paths (hook-enforced) |
| `.git/index.lock` exists | a background helper's read-only `git status` holds it for a second; a failed `./publish` then committed NONE of its paths | wait a few seconds and retry; never delete a lock younger than a minute; check `git status` after any failed publish |
| compound command refused whole | a `PreToolUse` hook (blanket stage, DLL stamp, sheet guard) refuses the entire Bash call before the shell runs — any file write chained before the commit never happened either | keep file writes and git commands in SEPARATE Bash calls; a hook's refusal means nothing in that call ran |
| zsh refspec modifier | `git push origin $N:refs/heads/main` — zsh reads `:r` as a modifier and mangles the refspec | `"${N}:refs/heads/main"` |
| land.sh duplicates | landing by plumbing leaves the clone "ahead N, behind M" with patch-equivalent copies; a stale clone shows phantom selftest reds (ledger_lint NOT_APPEND, a "lost" bridge tool) | `land.sh` now syncs itself; otherwise `./sync`. Re-check a red on a synced clone before fixing it |
| autostash | `pull --rebase --autostash` re-applied peers' dirty files and stranded 53 in `stash@{0}` (2026-10-10) | never stash; `./publish` and `./sync` use `reset --keep` |
| pre-push ledger lint judges the LOCAL HEAD | a correct plumbing push from a clone behind origin is refused NOT_APPEND | `./sync` first, then land |

# Runner selection

Claude is the default. Designer: `role_launch.py run-now --role Designer --runner codex --concept <dir> --by <seat> --why <reason> --apply`.
Relentless: set `runner: codex` in its rules JSON; Builder/Judge prompts and proof/verdict acceptance stay the same.

Whittle: `python3 "$WORKFLOWS_ROOT/whittle/run.py" --runner codex --cwd <project>`; Artisan: `RUNNER=codex LOGS=<logs> bash ralph/loop.sh`.
Set `RIMMANDRAKE_ROOT` to this clone and `WORKFLOWS_ROOT` to MandrakeWorkflows; see its `tools/RUNNERS.md` for setup.

Model comes from `codex_model` or `CODEX_MODEL`, then the CLI config; effort from `codex_effort` or `CODEX_EFFORT` (default high).
`codex_sandbox` / `CODEX_SANDBOX` defaults to workspace-write in code, but on Archmagi every agent gets `CODEX_SANDBOX=danger-full-access` from the environment (owner, 2026-11-09: *"Please grant that authority to all agents immediately."*; set in `~/.config/environment.d/50-codex-sandbox.conf`, `~/.zshenv` and `~/.profile`). The weekly `ops_watch.c_codex` meter must report MEASURED usage and reset; unreadable or >90% used refuses.

The isolated Designer smoke passed with that selection. Windows-launched WSL processes do not inherit Linux systemd filesystem walls; Judge confinement has no live certification here.

## Native WSL Codex as the live-game driver (proved 2026-11-10)

A native WSL `codex exec --sandbox danger-full-access` session drove the complete
Whittle pit-prison acceptance runner through Windows `python.exe`, then the
HugeThings P1 runner. No Claude runner or Claude tool call drove the game.
[The report](../../../../whittle/CODEX_LIVE_2026-11-10.md) links the raw attempts,
preflights, restoration receipts, independent pit judgment and published fixes.
This establishes launch → attach → disposable-site setup → real jobs/ticks →
occupied save/load → assertions → restoration → shutdown/release. It does not
certify general colony play, a full mod list, Windows sandbox confinement, mouse
interaction or flight. The Windows-launch workspace-write failures described
above remain separate from this native WSL result.

### What runs automatically, and what the operator must supply

`.claude/settings.json` is Claude configuration; Codex does not execute its
PreToolUse, Stop or SubagentStop hooks. Use the repository's tools and inspect
their results explicitly. In this session the operator supplied:

- The current owner authority, own-clone boundary, quota gate and source-first
  decisions. Run the task's `ops_watch.c_codex` reading before every unit and stop
  at the owner's cutoff (88% in this run). A native CLI process does not acquire
  the MandrakeWorkflows runner's quota gate just by being named Codex.
- The duties of `block_blind_scan`, `block_blanket_git_stage`,
  `block_shared_tree_merge`, `queue_lint`, `block_dll_source_mismatch` and
  `block_ledger_lint`: use the right instrument, explicit paths, one writer per
  clone, rimflow-only ledger writes, a published DLL with its matching `.srchash`,
  and append-only shards. Set this clone's noreply Git identity and
  `core.hooksPath=infrastructure/githooks`; Git-native guards then run for Codex
  too. Inspect failures: those guards explicitly fail open on some crashes.
  Other Claude art/canon/item-prose guards still apply when that work is touched;
  the live-driver authorization does not replace their requirements.
- Deploy planning, `--pull` rescue of unrecognized deployed edits, hold-file
  compliance, byte verification, intended tier selection and fresh process
  identity. These are operator/CLI contracts, not a side effect of saving source.
- Whittle completion and helper wrapup. Its Claude Stop hook normally checks
  DONE evidence, broaden work, judgment and freshness. Codex must run the workflow
  validator explicitly when using the full workflow and inspect any refusal;
  `whittle_stop.done_problems(...)` is the read-only claim check. Calling the Stop
  hook itself can move BLOCKED.md into history. This session used the authorized
  acceptance runner directly, kept the old blocked trial intact, and recorded
  new raw results plus a fresh independent judge; it does **not** claim a new
  complete Whittle orchestrator/Stop-hook run. Preserve raw receipts; never flip
  statuses or touch evidence merely to satisfy an mtime gate.
- Settings/snapshot debts, pilot diagnosis after three non-passes, exact readbacks,
  first-exception investigation, sane shutdown and immediate bridge release.
  Claude's helper `wrapup_hook` does not run automatically for a Codex helper.
  Keep the main driver responsible for cleanup even if a child exits.

`rimflow/driver_lock.py` now recognizes the nearest Codex **or** Claude ancestor.
Short-lived tool-shell PIDs no longer strand or invalidate a Codex lease.
`RM_DRIVER_PID` remains the explicit override; ordinarily let ancestor detection
work. Take only BENCH's bridge lease, never an OWNER hold. One process drives the
bridge at a time; read-only judges do not attach while the proof runs.

### Operating sequence used here

Run repository commands in this clone. Read `CLAUDE.md`, the charter, Git and game
state workflows and the deploy/bridge/live-proof skills first. The bridge tools
run in Windows Python; WSL Python runs offline checks and orchestration.

1. Check quota. Plan deployment with `deploy_custom_mods.py --mod <Mod>`, wait for
   its final summary and read every change. Before overwriting an unknown game
   edit, use `--pull <Mod>` and preserve its files/hashes outside the source tree;
   reconcile the rescued content deliberately. Use `winbuild.py <Mod>` for C#,
   keep the DLL/stamp pair, and publish completed changes through `./publish`.
2. `python3 src/RimMandrake/rimflow/cli.py bridge who`, then
   `bridge take --idle-ok --for "Codex live: <purpose>"`. A fresh clone may not yet
   have the ignored BRIDGE companion state; using the CLI establishes it. Verify
   the lease and stable driver identity before touching the game. Stop an old
   game with `northstar_driver.live_session.stop_game()` and stamp `./game --why
   "<reason>" down` before replacing assemblies. Apply only the reviewed deploy
   plan and require its VERIFIED byte comparison.
3. Use `modset_builder.py` for the smallest dependency-complete all-DLC tier while
   down. For the pit runner this was `flowworks` (12 mods). The HugeThings P1
   runner used the dynamic tier
   `mods__mandrake_rm_flowworks__mandrake_rm_hugethings__mandrake_rm_hugethingstestraces__mandrake_rm_patches`
   (14 mods). A deployed mod is not necessarily active. No owner-list restoration
   is owed; leave the tier useful for the next task. Check windowed/background
   preferences; do not focus/fullscreen the game or exercise flyer flight.
4. Run `preflight_bridge.py --tier quicktest --modset <tier> --deep --seat BENCH
   --json <receipt>` and require GREEN. The preflight **tier** selects checks;
   **modset** selects the intended list. Omitting modset can accidentally judge a
   quick test against the full list. Missing inputs are UNMEASURED, never green.
   Resolve dependency changes by actual LoadFolders/version/assembly provenance,
   then explicitly accept an investigated new baseline; never bypass fingerprints.
5. `./game --why "<reason>" loading` is a **ledger stamp**, not a launcher. Launch
   with `northstar_driver.live_session.launch_and_wait()`: it uses Steam, waits
   within the configured Steam-to-process budget, then the process-to-bridge
   deadline against a fresh log cursor. A successful Steam command is not proof
   that its process already exists. Never launch the bare game executable.
6. Run the same preflight with `--live`; require one fresh process, listening
   bridge, actual ordered running list and companion/deployed identity. Read
   Player.log's first exception **and Config error lines**. L03's missing-type
   gate can be GREEN while its reason reports nonfatal config errors. Fix those
   causes too. Stamp `./game --why "<reason>" up` after attaching successfully.
7. Run the acceptance script through this clone's UNC path, for example:

   ```sh
   python.exe "$(wslpath -w "$PWD/src/RimMandrake/FlowWorks/northstar/concept_scenes.py")" \
     --out "$(wslpath -w "$PWD/whittle/evidence/codex-live/new-relative.json")"
   ```

   Use an existing disposable registered save, never worldgen or a canonical
   save. A guarded scene-begin save must appear under a new name without changing
   an existing save; reload it before taking the baseline and in `finally`.
   Compare the restored rectangle/settings, not just load success. Preserve
   occupied fixtures on occupied reload. Use governed real ticks, exact deltas,
   declared fixture identities and explicitly restored isolation controls.
8. Read failed tool payloads and the **first** Player.log exception before fixing
   the mod. Separate MOD, SITE and HARNESS causes. A successful order is not a
   running job, and a successful batch is not its requested cardinality. Keep
   positive and disabled controls. At three non-passes obtain independent pilot
   diagnosis before repeating. Build/deploy/restart for changed C# or XML, then
   rerun; never relabel an old receipt. Obtain a fresh independent Whittle judge
   from the frozen statement and raw evidence, without builder conclusions.
9. Record the result on the ledger item. `verify --criterion` only counts against
   the registered build SHA: publish the tested artifact, update `implemented`
   with the **unchanged** owed criteria, then verify at that SHA. Do not claim a
   different SHA was tested just to close it. Publish the explicit ledger shard.
   Restore settings and snapshots even on failure; if broken, stop and stamp
   DOWN. On completion, stop/stamp DOWN and release immediately. Verify both
   `rimflow bridge who` and its host driver lock are FREE before offline work.

A fresh clone's ignored JawaBench comparison artifact may be absent. Recover it
only after checking the installed assembly's embedded source hash against this
clone, or build it by the companion workflow. This run recovered the matching
ignored artifact without redeploying it. The missing `.srchash` warning remains
visible; this is not a claim of versioned companion provenance. The tested mod
DLLs retain their own checked stamps. Keep token-bearing full logs private.

### Stalls, fixes and lessons from this run

Each row has a filed lesson; the report preserves failed attempts alongside the
accepted receipts. These were not reasons to skip a check.

| Observed trap | Cause and repair | Lesson file under `infrastructure/state/lessons/` |
|---|---|---|

| Proof transport/work-type assumptions | Match actual static arguments, `PatientBedRest` and returned order contracts | `20261111T031500Z-BENCH-pit-proof-transport-contract.md` |
| Generated warden cannot do care work | Bounded Baseliner fixture selection; verify all required enabled work types and food supply | `20261111T032108Z-BENCH-pit-prison-capable-fixtures.md` |
| Tending helper cannot find a worker | Select registered WorkGiverDefs, not an exact base worker class | `20261111T032704Z-BENCH-registered-tending-workgiver.md` |
| Prisoners disappear after occupied load | Default site cleanup removes hostile-faction pawns; request only modal-broker controls for occupied snapshots | `20261111T034115Z-BENCH-occupied-load-vanishes-prisoners.md` |
| Governor removes the expected staged hostiles | Declare only those fixture IDs, withdraw only owned declarations; retain unrelated danger stops | `20261111T034500Z-BENCH-declare-hostile-proof-fixtures.md` |
| Python-only repair restages a slow C# suite | Split fast driver faults from retained production math checks | `20261111T034836Z-BENCH-separate-fast-pit-driver-tests.md` |
| Upright inmate sleeps beside delivered food | Probe while rested before the day; explicitly require the awake fixture precondition | `20261111T035901Z-BENCH-awake-not-only-not-downed.md` |
| Normal berserk stops an isolated mechanism proof | Apply/read back standard quiet flags across reloads, restore exact prior flags; no random-event claim | `20261111T041023Z-BENCH-isolated-prison-proof-random-events.md` |
| New care order is accepted but queued | Stop the previous worker job, require real returned care job to be current before ticking | `20261111T042221Z-BENCH-care-clock-requires-running-job.md` |
| Valid passes do not discharge old-build criteria | Register the repaired published artifact before verifying its unchanged criteria | `20261111T043944Z-BENCH-acceptance-build-sha.md` |
| Harness plant counted as an elephant race | Select resolved race definitions, keep exact expected race controls | `20261111T044005Z-BENCH-harness-thingdef-not-race.md` |
| Existing test races produce config errors | ThingDef names cannot end in digits; rename both fixture races/kinds and callers to `*Adult` | `20261111T044400Z-BENCH-harness-def-numeric-ending.md` |

| 100 artboard subjects become one | Artboard rows use newlines, not semicolons; assert returned count and every row | `20261111T044944Z-BENCH-artboard-batch-needs-newlines.md` |

T3 retry/butcher controls with occupied reload. Large Pawns live clearance,

# RimWorld modding

Patches fail *silently*, XML comments have a syntax rule most people don't know,
and a single bad Def entry can kill three unrelated mods at startup with an error
that names none of them. Almost every hour lost here is lost to writing something
plausible instead of reading something real.

The method: **find the ground truth on disk, write the smallest change that
survives a mod being absent, prove it before shipping, and record what you
learned.**

---

## 1. Read the real file first. Always.

Before writing a line of a patch, open the def you are patching and the def you
are patching *around* — the actual XML in the actual mod folder that is loaded
right now, not the wiki's version and not what a project doc said last month.

→ the grep command: `references/traps-xml-and-defs.md`.

This costs thirty seconds. Three specific reasons it matters more here than
elsewhere:

- **A failed PatchOperation is a no-op, not an error you'll notice.** It prints
  one line into a log with thousands of lines. Nothing breaks. The patch just
  never happened. You will believe it worked.
- **Def names are redefined by other mods.** The `Armadillo` you're looking at
  in Core may not be the `Armadillo` that wins. Last loaded def with a given
  `defName` replaces earlier ones entirely.
- **Fields move between versions.** `<wildness>` was valid on `RaceProperties`
  and isn't in 1.6. Read `XML error: <field> doesn't correspond to any field in
  type X` as a **version-drift** report, not a typo: the mod predates the game,
  the value is dropped, the def loads anyway, and the instance count is the
  severity (eight of them = eight races quietly wrong). Wikis lag by a version.
⚠️ Full caveat (the `wildness`/`leatherLabel` corpse-gen crash) moved: `references/traps-xml-and-defs.md`.

When you find the ground truth, **quote its file path and the exact snippet in a
comment at the top of the patch**, with a date. Future-you re-reads that comment
instead of re-doing the search.

- **One negative observation is not a mechanism: read the consuming code before filing the fix.** When a write reports success and nothing changes, or an expected thing is absent, the next action is to read the mechanism, not to write the finding. A wrong mechanism yields a finding that is internally coherent, survives review and gets acted on (four filed findings each died on one direct check: a census that read `Defs/` while the content sat in `Patches/`; a tool run at a settled game; `FactionGenerator.InitializeFactions` early-returning when a faction list is passed; a `def` field read once at worldgen and never at draw time). `mcp__rimsage__search_source` and `mcp__rimsage__read_csharp_symbol` (`typeName` plus optional `memberName`) read the real C# in one call: before filing any item whose fix depends on "field X does Y", paste the consuming method into the item. A single tile or click cannot settle anything whose commonness is a few percent. When a filed finding is refuted, drop the item in the same action: a corrected item left in the queue with an explanatory header is a landmine with a note taped to it, because people read the spec before the note.
- **The cheapest disproof is a control artifact you never touched.** When data you produced looks corrupted (181 of 744 authored weights read 0), find the nearest instance you did NOT produce and look at it: a vanilla biome the project does not patch showed the same zeros, so the pipeline was innocent and every theory about it was wasted. It is one read, and it beats a subagent, which comes back repeating the theory it was handed. If the owner pushes back ("I'm not sure I believe this"), go find the mechanism rather than re-running the same probe.
- **For animal and def data the three sources are the offline `Defs/` scan, the live dump and `Player.log`, and the join is the deliverable.** The offline scan (`Utils/animal_inventory.py`) answers "what did the author write, and where do I patch it" and is the only source with provenance (mod, file, xpath). The live dump (`mods/dev/RimDefDump`, a C# startup mod) answers "what exists at runtime", post-patch and post-override. `Player.log` is negative space only (~15 dangling cross-references and ~22 config errors on a full load); it does not enumerate defs, and the huge `[Source: X]/[File: Y]` blocks are the "Possible Matches" hint under each error, not a load trace. Join them with `Utils/animal_live_diff.py`. RimBridge cannot dump the def database (no `list_defs`/`get_def`, `run_lua` forbids CLR access, vanilla `DebugOutputsEcology` tables render to a dialog, not the log), hence the C# mod: do not re-litigate. A 0% coverage column is far more likely a dead xpath than an empty field (1.6 dropped fields four columns read; see DEAD XPATHS in `animal_inventory.py`).

## 3. Pick the implementation tier before you pick the code

Most "how do I do X in RimWorld" questions are really "at which layer does X
belong". Getting this wrong is expensive — people write a C# mod for something a
six-line XML patch does, or try to patch a def for something that only exists at
runtime. Work down this ladder and stop at the first tier that can do the job:

| Tier | Layer | Use when the thing must… | Cost to change later |
|---|---|---|---|
| a | Mod list / settings / scenario | be true before worldgen | free |
| b | XML Def patch | be *true of the game* — stats, spawns, recipes, names | cheap |
| c | C# / Harmony assembly | *behave* differently — new mechanics, new AI | expensive |
| d | Save-game edit | be true of one existing colony, retroactively | one-shot, risky |
| e | Live runtime manipulation (bridge/console) | *change during play* | ephemeral |
| f | External host-side tooling | analyse or generate outside the game | free |

The rule of thumb that keeps this straight: **bake what must be TRUE, script
what must be PLACED, run live only what must CHANGE.** If a value never varies
during a playthrough, it belongs in tier b, full stop. Reaching for C# because
XML feels weak is the single most common overbuild in this domain.

⚠️ **Prove a comp exists before scoping tier b around it:** `grep -rln
"CompProperties_<Name>" "$RW/Data"`. Zero hits means the mechanic is stat-driven
or hard-coded in the `thingClass` — there is no `CompProperties_ShieldBelt` in
1.6; `Apparel_ShieldBelt` is plain `Apparel` and the shield is entirely
`EnergyShieldEnergyMax` + `EnergyShieldRechargeRate`. Zero hits moves the job to
tier c, which rides a game load alone instead of batching.

## 4. Writing an XML patch

### The shape to default to

Every operation goes inside a `PatchOperationConditional` that tests for the
exact node you are about to touch. This is not ceremony — it is what makes a
patch safe when a mod is absent, when the user updates it, or when the author
fixes the bug upstream. An unconditional patch against a missing node prints a
red error at every launch and trains the user to ignore red errors.
→ the same conditional-wrapped example, worked in full: `references/patch-operations.md`.

Keep the test xpath and the inner xpath **identical** unless you have a stated
reason: differing ones test for one thing and modify another.

## 5. Validate before you deploy

Run the bundled validator on any patch file before it goes near the Mods folder.
It catches the silent failures, which otherwise cost a full game restart to find.

```bash
python3 scripts/validate_patch.py path/to/Patch.xml \
    --defs "C:/Program Files (x86)/Steam/steamapps/common/RimWorld/Data" \
    --defs "C:/Program Files (x86)/Steam/steamapps/workshop/content/294100" \
    --defs "C:/Program Files (x86)/Steam/steamapps/common/RimWorld/Mods"
```

🔴 **Pass the Mods folder too** — first-party mods live there, not in Workshop
content (`references/patch-operations.md` has the failure this avoids).

The valuable check is the last one: it **runs each xpath against the real Defs on
disk and reports how many nodes it hits**. Zero hits means the patch would silently
do nothing; more hits than expected means a `Remove` is about to take out more than
you think. (Its other five checks are in `references/patch-operations.md`.)

A patch that validates clean can still be wrong about *intent*, so also confirm
in-game: load, then check the dev console (or `Player.log`) for the patch's own
name. Silence is success.

### Two things it cannot see

It reads defs **unpatched**, so a node another mod creates at runtime is invisible
and **0 matches can be the correct answer**; and it checks field names in no file,
so a hand-authored Def with a field that moved between versions sails straight
through. Both are in `references/patch-operations.md`, with the WeatherDef that
shipped a renamed field.

## 6. Deploying

Author in the project repo, deploy a copy to the game. Never edit in place under
`Mods/` — that copy is disposable, overwritten by the next deploy, and not in
version control.

**The full procedure is `skills/rimworld-deploy/SKILL.md`**: the plan-first
`deploy_custom_mods.py` run, reading the plan before `--apply`, `-` lines and
`--pull`, `DEPLOY_HOLD.txt`, the minimum viable mod folder, why compatibility
patches must be enabled LAST in load order, and the restart that follows.

🔴 **Deployed is not live.** RimWorld reads defs **once, at launch**, so the process
start time is the def-read time and anything newer under `Mods/` is not loaded. Before
you call anything live, inspect the CONSUMER, and run the pre-flight of the deployed
copy against the mod list it will actually load with:
**`references/deploying-and-liveness.md`** — the mtime check, map-gen defs needing a
NEW map, the `MayRequire` gate that outlived its mod, and why `validate_patch.py`'s
`0 errors` cannot prove independence from a mod you are about to remove.

## 7. Debugging from Player.log

`%USERPROFILE%\AppData\LocalLow\Ludeon Studios\RimWorld by Ludeon Studios\Player.log`

Triage by **consequence, not by position in the file**. The ladder, worst first:
static-constructor / `TypeInitializationException` / `ReflectionTypeLoadException`
(the mod is *dead*, not noisy) → `Could not execute post-long-event action` (costs
exactly that one action; the queue continues) → `Could not resolve cross-reference`
(benign **or** fatal — it depends entirely on the `wanter`) →
`Patch operation … failed` (a no-op) → translation and sound errors (cosmetic).

⚠️ **The op named in a patch error is the WRAPPER, not the failure.**
`PatchOperationFindMod(Asimov) failed` was a broken *inner* `Replace`, not a
missing Asimov: `FindMod` returns the inner result while `ToString()` prints the
outer, and a genuinely absent mod returns **true** and logs nothing at all. Read
the inner op — and note that a field sitting at its C# default (`isOrganic`) has
no node for `Replace` to find, which is why `Conditional` is the safe default.

**`references/player-log-triage.md` has each rung in full: the greps, the IL-level
evidence for what each error actually costs, the two shapes of cross-reference
damage, and the judged-safe list you must keep.** Open it whenever you are reading
a log — five "benign" cross-reference lines were the sole cause of a dead mod for
three loads running, and a `ReflectionTypeLoadException` is usually load order
rather than a broken assembly.

## 8. C# mods, briefly

Reach for C# only when tier (c) is genuinely required — see §3. When you do,
`references/csharp-and-loading.md` covers Harmony patch types, the entry-point
classes and their required constructor signatures, and `LoadFolders.xml`. Two
constructor rules cause a disproportionate share of "mod does nothing" reports:

- A `GameComponent` needs a **public constructor taking `(Game game)`**. Without
  it, `Game.FillComponents` throws `MissingMethodException` and the component
  silently never exists — worse than a crash, because the feature appears to
  work and simply has no consequences.
- A `Mod` subclass needs `(ModContentPack content)`.

🔴 **Every mod we ship carries a real Mod Settings screen** (owner ruling,
2026-09-12, `MOD_OPTIONS_RETROFIT_1`): on/off per major feature or mechanic,
tuning where a number is the experience, defaults equal to shipped behaviour,
all-off degrading gracefully, and any worldgen-affecting toggle labelled as
such. Biome-kit mechanics get feature-gated so they can be enabled in a
different biome without the whole kit. This is standard `Mod` +
`ModSettings` — a settings class holding the fields, a `Mod` subclass
exposing `DoSettingsWindowContents` and calling `settings.Write()`, and every
gated feature reading its own field rather than a hardcoded constant.
Applies to every mod going forward, not just a retrofit pass.

⚠️ **`FilthMaker` refuses `Filth_AnimalFilth` on ALL natural terrain**
(`placementMask [Terrain]` vs `filthAcceptanceMask [Unnatural]`) — a comp's
filth drop is a silent no-op outdoors, and "the comp ticked with no filth
appearing" is not evidence the comp is broken.

⚠️ **A subprocess wrapper that only reads `stderr` on a nonzero exit can miss
the real error entirely if the process writes it to `stdout` instead.** A C#
wrapper around an external CLI produced an empty, useless diagnostic on a real
auth failure because that failure printed to stdout, not stderr. Capture and
surface BOTH streams on any subprocess failure; never assume the error
channel.

---
- **C# builds work from WSL; do not believe "this WSL machine cannot compile the .csproj".** There is no Visual Studio, NuGet CLI or .NET Framework targeting pack, and none is needed. The SDK is user-local at `C:\Users\Mandrake\.dotnet\dotnet.exe` (no admin, not on PATH; `C:\Program Files\dotnet` is runtime-only and will not build). From WSL: `/mnt/c/Users/Mandrake/.dotnet/dotnet.exe build 'D:\Luke\dev\Rimworld\src\...\Foo.csproj' -c Release` (forward-slash binary, Windows-style project path) builds clean with no setup. `net472` targeting comes from the `Microsoft.NETFramework.ReferenceAssemblies` NuGet package. Reference the game's DLLs in `RimWorldWin64_Data\Managed` with `<Private>false</Private>` so nothing is copied into the mod folder. Copy `mods/dev/RimDefDump/Source/RimDefDump.csproj` as the working reference. Any subagent brief that touches C# must state the invocation explicitly: the false "can't compile from WSL" claim, shipping C# build-unverified, is the most common false claim subagents produce.

## Handing over something you cannot check yourself

🔴 **First ask whether it needs the game at all.** The default is source — the def, the
patch, the C#, the capture, `measure`, an `md5sum`. If you cannot say in one line what
source cannot tell you, verify it yourself and close the item.

A live check owes three lines: **the call**, **the expected reading**, and **how a pass
could be false**. Name a positive observation, never "no error" — an absence is the
cheapest thing to produce by accident.

🔑 Whoever proves it **closes** it — no hand-back — then greps
`infrastructure/state/items/` for what else it settled.
**`references/validation-plan.md`** has the rule and the four false passes.

## 9. Keep this skill learning

**The live log is `references/traps-*.md`.** Open the one topic file that matches
what you are about to do — patches, tooling, art, the mod stack, or diagnosis.
Reading all five is not the intent and costs ~25k tokens.

**If you are already running, do not reread — take the delta.** `python3
src/RimMandrake/Utils/whats_new.py --seat <SEAT>` prints what peers appended, in a
few lines instead of ~25k tokens. Run it when the game loads.

**After any RimWorld task, ask: did anything here surprise me?** If yes, append it
to the matching topic file, short: what it looked like, what was actually true,
what worked. ⚠️ **Most candidate lessons should be REJECTED** — it goes in only if
it is specific, non-obvious, RimWorld-bound and still true. General software or
process advice is not a trap. If it changes what *this file* says to do by
default, it belongs here instead, and does not get logged at all.

🔴 **Never number an entry, and never cite one by number, line or heading.** Say
"as per the trap file" and stop. Editing an installed skill changes nothing
durable: edit the copy in the user's project, re-package, and say it has been
**delivered** rather than saved.

# Deploying to the game

## 1. "Written" and "the game can see it" are two claims

```
<repo>/custom_patches/<ModName>/   ← source of truth, committed
        ↓  deploy_custom_mods.py
C:\Program Files (x86)\Steam\steamapps\common\RimWorld\Mods\<ModName>   ← what loads
```

The game names its own copy on every launch:
`Adding mandrake.jawa.patches(C:\...\RimWorld\Mods\Jawa_Patches)`.

**Nothing syncs them.** Editing only the repo means the change silently never
reaches the game — no error, no red text, the def simply is not there. That cost a
whole test cycle once: a xenotype and its pawnkinds authored, reported ready, and
invisible in game because the deployed copy was untouched. **And never edit in
place under `Mods/`** — that copy is disposable, overwritten by the next `--apply`,
and not in version control.

🔑 **Where you run it.** Edit and commit in your seat clone (`/home/mandrake/rm/<seat>`);
`deploy_custom_mods.py` runs from the clone and plans/copies from it. C# mods are built with
`python3 src/RimMandrake/Utils/winbuild.py <Mod|csproj>` (stages on `D:\ClaudeWork\rimmandrake\build`, Windows
dotnet, DLL and `.srchash` copied back as a pair). `D:\Luke\dev\RimMandrake` is a read-only
mirror of origin/main: Windows tools read it, nothing writes it.

🔴 **A subagent's clean `dotnet build`/`validate_patch.py` pass, plus a real
commit+push, is NOT proof the fix was deployed.** Twice in one wave a
genuinely-fixed patch/DLL sat undeployed in the repo while a live re-test still
showed the old failure. Deploying static def/XML output needs no running game —
always run `deploy_custom_mods.py --mod <X>` (plan-only first) before trusting a
live re-check of anything a prior pass claims fixed.

🔑 **"Deployed" and "active" are separate states with nothing reconciling
them.** `deploy_custom_mods.py` writes files and (correctly) never touches the
mod list — it even PRINTS "not enabled in ModsConfig" where nobody reads it. A
mod can be deployed and inert (present on disk, absent from `ModsConfig.xml`,
so it silently never spawns anything) for a long time before anyone notices;
check both states independently, never infer one from the other.

## 2. Plan first. Always read the plan.

```bash
python src/RimMandrake/Utils/deploy_custom_mods.py                 # plan only -- changes nothing
python src/RimMandrake/Utils/deploy_custom_mods.py --apply         # repo -> game, then self-verifies
python src/RimMandrake/Utils/deploy_custom_mods.py --mod Jawa_Patches
python src/RimMandrake/Utils/deploy_custom_mods.py --apply --prune # also delete deployed files gone from the repo
```

Safe by default, skips authoring-side files (`Source/`, `*.py`, `README.md`), warns
when a mod is not enabled in `ModsConfig.xml`, verifies every copy, and exits
non-zero while drift remains — so the plan doubles as a pre-flight check.

🔴 **`--apply` overwrites the game copy with whatever is in the repo *right now*,
including another seat's half-finished work.** Five seats share this tree.

> **Read the plan. `--apply` only if every listed file is yours.** A file you do not
> recognise is a live hazard, not a todo — tell the owner before you write.

⚠️ **With no `--mod`, the walk is alphabetical and a 120s tool-call timeout can
TRUNCATE it mid-list.** A run that stopped at "Cuisine" would have been read as
"only Armoury drifts"; the real answer that day was 5 mods including one the
caller owned. Redirect the run to a file and confirm it printed its final
`Drift found` / `Everything in sync` line before believing any drift list.

More traps for this section: [references/traps.md](references/traps.md) § 2. Plan first. Always read the plan..

## 3. A `-` line means someone hand-edited the deployed copy

`-` = present in the game, absent from the repo: an edit made directly in `Mods/`
that `--apply` is about to destroy.

```bash
python src/RimMandrake/Utils/deploy_custom_mods.py --pull <ModName>   # game -> repo, rescue it first
```

`--pull` before overwriting, every time.

## 4. Validate BEFORE it goes near the Mods folder — BOTH flags

```bash
python skills/rimworld-modding/scripts/validate_patch.py <file> \
  --live <dump> \
  --defs "C:/Program Files (x86)/Steam/steamapps/common/RimWorld/Data" \
  --defs "C:/Program Files (x86)/Steam/steamapps/workshop/content/294100" \
  --defs "C:/Program Files (x86)/Steam/steamapps/common/RimWorld/Mods"
```

🔴 **The Mods folder is not optional.** First-party `mandrake.*` mods live
there, not in Workshop content — omit it and a real, working cross-mod
`ParentName` inheritance reports as "resolves to no def" (a false failure).

⚠️ **`--live` and `--defs` are orthogonal, and only `--defs` checks xpaths.**
`--live` checks defName existence; `--defs` walks the XML and reports xpath hit
counts. `validate_patch.py <file> --live <dump>` prints `OK - 0 errors` having
evaluated **zero xpaths**, and says so above: `no --defs given; static checks only`.
**If only `--live` ran, nothing was validated.**

🔴 **`measure` is not executable on the Mac laptop** (`permission denied`) and
there is no local def dump there either — "does this def resolve against the
live mod list" is UNMEASURABLE from the laptop. Say so and hand the check to a
session on the Windows Desktop rather than closing the item on an assumption
(2026-09-22).

⚠️ **`--defs` inherits the LIVE `ModsConfig.xml`**, which another seat may have cut
to a spike. Pass the **newest** backup, never a pinned filename, and never a small
spike config — every xpath then legitimately matches nothing and the wall of false
failures burns a day:

```bash
--mods-config infrastructure/state/modlists/ModsConfig.FULL.LATEST.xml
```

🔴 **CORRECTED 2026-08-22 by CHECK — the command this section used to give was
`$(ls -t deployed/config/ModsConfig.full-*.xml | head -1)`, and it resolved to the
WRONG STACK.** Measured on the day: that glob returns
`deployed/config/ModsConfig.full-574.2026-08-12.xml` — **574 mods, ten days old, and
it still carries `thereallemon.factioncontrol`**, a mod the owner removed on
2026-08-21 because it aborted three save loads. The live list is **578 and clean**.

The advice ("pass the newest backup, never a pinned filename") was right; the command
was globbing the wrong directory. `deployed/config/` is an ARCHIVE of dated snapshots
and its newest member is only as fresh as the last time someone happened to write one
there. **`infrastructure/state/modlists/ModsConfig.FULL.LATEST.xml` is the owner's
real list** — it is what `modlist_swap.py --restore` restores FROM (`modlist_swap.py:24`),
so it is maintained rather than merely deposited.

⚠️ **It is still not the LIVE file.** Confirm they agree before trusting a verdict:
```bash
diff <(grep -o '<li>[^<]*</li>' infrastructure/state/modlists/ModsConfig.FULL.LATEST.xml) \
     <(grep -o '<li>[^<]*</li>' "/mnt/c/Users/Mandrake/AppData/LocalLow/Ludeon Studios/RimWorld by Ludeon Studios/Config/ModsConfig.xml")
```

Read the `N active mods → M def files` line before trusting any verdict. **If it does
not say 578, you are validating against a stack the game does not load.** 0 errors
is the bar.

⚠️ **It reads `Patches/` only — never `Defs/`.** New content under `Defs/` is
unvalidated, so parse every XML in the mod folder yourself, `About.xml` included.

More traps for this section: [references/traps.md](references/traps.md) § 4. Validate BEFORE it goes near the Mods folder — BOTH flags.

## 5. Files undeployed ON PURPOSE — `DEPLOY_HOLD.txt`

`src/DEPLOY_HOLD.txt` is read by the deploy script; anything matching is
reported **HELD** instead of as drift, and `--apply` will not write it.

```
<glob>    # <reason, including who ruled it and when>
```

Paths are relative to `src/`, forward slashes, and **`*` matches across
directory separators** — `WreckedMachines/*` holds the whole tree.

**A reason is REQUIRED.** Without one the plan can only say "the repo and the game
differ": *parked on purpose* and *half-finished* render identically, and both end
with "Drift found. Re-run with `--apply`." Acting on that overrides an owner ruling
while looking like housekeeping. **It is PER-FILE, not per-mod** — a live mod can
have two held files while the rest of it keeps deploying, and inferring the hold
from `ModsConfig.xml` only proves a mod is INERT, never that it is INTENDED.

🔑 **"Not in the Workshop folder" is not "not available."** Donor mod sources
are vendored at `vendor/mod_sources/` — check there before concluding a donor
mod's own XML/source is unreachable.

More traps for this section: [references/traps.md](references/traps.md) § 5. Files undeployed ON PURPOSE — `DEPLOY_HOLD.txt`.

## 6. Not every folder is deployable

**A mod with no `About/About.xml`, or no `packageId` in it, is not a mod.**
Deploying it creates a `Mods/` folder RimWorld ignores; the plan flags
`no packageId in About.xml`. That is **a ruling to ask for, not a file to invent** —
a packageId is an identity, and guessing one ships a name nobody chose. Hold the
mod with its reason and put the decision in the owner's path. Minimum viable folder:

⚠️ **That refusal message can point at the wrong field.** It also fires when
`ET.parse` throws on a genuinely malformed `About.xml` — a raw `<=`/`<` inside
plain description text parses as a tag start (`harvestAfterGrowth <= 0f` written
straight into a description broke one this way). The tool refused correctly; the
message named `packageId` when the real defect was that the file does not parse
at all. Check the file actually parses before assuming the packageId is absent.

🔴 **`[ -e "$dir" ]` is not a test for "a mod lives here."** `src/RimMandrake/Pits`
passed that test while holding only `__pycache__` — the mod had merged elsewhere
and the folder was a shell. Test `$dir/About/About.xml` instead; existence of a
directory is not identity of a mod.

```
<ModName>/
├── About/About.xml          (packageId, name, supportedVersions, description)
└── Patches/<Something>.xml  (or Defs/ for new content)
```

More traps for this section: [references/traps.md](references/traps.md) § 6. Not every folder is deployable.

## 7. Assemblies deploy in the shutdown window, not now

A DLL the game has loaded **cannot be written while RimWorld runs** — memory-mapped,
and Windows refuses with `WinError 1224`. The copy is impossible, not merely
ineffective. Deploy in the gap after the game closes and before it launches, and
tell CHECK before any shutdown: `skills/rimworld-load-round/SKILL.md` §6.

🔴 **`deploy_custom_mods.py --mod <X>` deploys only that one mod, not the mods it
depends on.** A new mod referencing a class from a SIBLING mod's assembly (a
`<li Class="RimMandrake.SomeNamespace.SomeExtension">` pointing at another mod's
compiled comp) got enabled and deployed while the DEPENDENCY mod's own rebuilt
DLL had never actually been redeployed — confirmed by comparing deployed-vs-repo
DLL mtimes (the deployed copy was hours stale). A stale dependency DLL missing a
referenced type can crash mod-loading badly enough to trip RimWorld's own
corrupted-mods safety net (§ below), resetting `ModsConfig.xml` — not just log a
quiet config error. **When enabling a mod that leans on another mod's C# (a
shared "engine" assembly), deploy BOTH mods explicitly before the next launch.**

⚠️ **But `WinError 1224` is not the only lock failure, and the other one is
silent.** `deploy_custom_mods.py --apply` has printed the DLL's `~` plan line
and "Deployed N file(s)" while silently SKIPPING a locked assembly — the file
count printed is the only tell that it did not match the plan-line count.
Mechanism: a TRUNCATING copy (`shutil.copy2`, `open(dst, "wb")`) fails on a
locked file with `[Errno 22] Invalid argument` while an in-place
`open(dst, "r+b")` write + `os.truncate` lands byte-identical. Without the
in-place route, the XML half of a deploy lands and the DLL half silently does
not — which discards every def whose comp `Class` lives in that DLL. Re-run
once the game is really gone, and check the deployed vs. plan file counts
before trusting either "Deployed" line.

⚠️ **`MayRequire` checks the MOD, never the TYPE — it is no protection against
an assembly that is PRESENT but STALE.** New C# written and never rebuilt can
leave types missing from the deployed DLL while every `Class=` reference
guards correctly on the mod being active: the guard passes, the type still
isn't there, and the def carrying it is silently discarded. Check that the
type is actually IN the deployed DLL's bytes, not merely that the owning mod
is active. (2026-09-21)

## 7b. 🔴 Is this artifact CURRENT? Never answer from a timestamp

Half the deploy questions in this project are really one question — *does this
derived thing still describe what the game loads?* — and reading **age** to answer
it has now been wrong four separate times in one day. The rule:

> **Trust a fingerprint of the load-set. Never a clock, on any layer:
> folder mtime, file mtime, or the artifact's own captured timestamp.**

Each of these was believed, acted on, and false:

| the reading | why it lied |
|---|---|
| **A folder's mtime** | `DefDump/defs/` read `Aug 14` while every file inside was written `Aug 15`. A dump that **overwrites a fixed set of filenames** creates and deletes nothing, so the directory mtime never moves. Generalises to any tool that rewrites the same names. |
| **The artifact's own `capturedUtc`** | Fresh in TIME is not fresh in SET. A dump captured 08:10 missed a mod deprecated at 11:58. **Direction matters**: that dump is a *superset* — everything live is described correctly, but it still carries defs from a mod that no longer loads, so an xpath onto *those* validates **clean** and matches **nothing** in game. |
| **A bare `<li>` count in `ModsConfig.xml`** | Reads 580 against a true 575. The file holds a second list, `knownExpansions`, duplicating the DLC ids. **Scope the count inside `<activeMods>`.** |
| **`Version.txt`** | Reads `rev590` while every engine-written file reads `rev591`. **The build stamp comes from the RUNNING game**, not from the file that appears to name it. (BUILD, 2026-08-15) |
| **A flat `DefDump/manifest.json` reader** | Silently degrades to `Version.txt` since the dump layout migrated to `captures/` — the flat path is gone, the reader finds nothing, and it resurfaces the exact rev590/591 lie one row up. `sync_mod_state.py` nearly stamped `rev590` over `rev591` saves before this was caught (fixed `801bd127`; swept as `FLAT_MANIFEST_READER_SWEEP_1`). |
| **`refresh.py` calling `defs.sqlite` "current"** | `DumpDB.stale` checks the mod-set **fingerprint**, not whether the capture it names still **exists on disk**. Retention had already PRUNED the source capture (built 08-23) while a newer one existed (08-29); the fingerprint still matched, so the verdict read current anyway. Rebuild whenever provenance names a missing capture — a matching fingerprint is not proof the file behind it survives (BENCH 2026-08-29). |
| **A generator's own "regenerating is a no-op" header comment** | Can drift silently from a renamed/moved target and never say so. `gen_pawnkind_roster.py`'s own claim was stale — it emitted pre-rename defNames across 49 `PawnKindDef`s, and a routine re-run per the file's own instructions would have silently reverted a whole naming migration. **Verify a generator's no-op claim with `git diff --stat` against committed output, never the exit code** (2026-09-18). |

✅ **What was right the whole time: `refresh.py`'s `STALE` verdict**, because it
keys on the load-set fingerprint rather than the clock — and it named the one real
mod while two seats were escalating the wrong thing. **Believe it over your own
timestamp arithmetic.**

⬜ **Coverage is a third axis, after time and set.** 79 of 529 def-type files in
the 2026-08-15 dump are **empty** (`AbilityDef` among them), so for those types
"absent from the dump" says nothing at all about the game. A `--defs` check
against an empty type is **UNMEASURED, not passed** — give it its own exit code
and its own word, or it silently becomes a green tick.

📌 Dump location, freshness and known holes are published by the seat that
measures them: `observed/LIVE.md`. **Read it; do not
re-derive it**, and do not copy its numbers into another doc where they will rot.

More traps for this section: [references/traps.md](references/traps.md) § 7b. 🔴 Is this artifact CURRENT? Never answer from a timestamp.

## 8. After deploying

- **Restart RimWorld.** Defs are parsed once at startup; reloading a save does not
  pick up new XML. Adding brand-new defs is safe for an existing save; changing or
  removing a def a save already references is not.
- **Enable compatibility-patch mods LAST in load order.** Patches apply in load
  order, so a fix-up mod loading before the mod it fixes patches a def that has not
  been redefined yet, and the redefine wins. This is the most common reason a
  correct patch appears to do nothing.
- **One mod at a time**, verified before the next — `skills/rimworld-load-round/SKILL.md` §3.
- Test on a dev-mode throwaway world and read `Player.log` for the patch's own name
  before trusting it in the campaign save.
- 🔴 **"Deployed and VERIFIED" is true only until the next writer.** Every clone
  deploys to the same Mods folder: a subagent's verified UtinniPatches deploy was
  overwritten within minutes by another clone deploying from an older sha. Before
  calling a fix live, re-run the deploy dry run from a clone AT the fix sha — a
  clean plan (no `~`/`-` lines for your files) is the proof; the earlier report is not.

More traps for this section: [references/traps.md](references/traps.md) § 8. After deploying.

## 9. Validation plan — what you owe whoever holds the game

**A deploy ends with a validation plan, not with `--apply`.** You are almost never
the seat that will see it work: a game load costs **23–30 minutes** and one game is
shared by five seats, so whoever holds it needs your prediction, not a nudge to
"have a look at the Jawa stuff".

### The six fields

**1. The observable** — what a player SEES when it works. 🔴 A positive
observation, never "no error"; absences are the cheapest thing in the world to
produce by accident.
**2. The route** — the exact call, defName or click path that produces it.
**3. The prediction** — a number or specific string, written BEFORE the look.
**4. The threshold** — what CLOSES it, and the minutia explicitly out of scope. An
item with no threshold is inspected forever; one observation, not a battery.
**5. Batch or solo** — most checks ride together; **a new assembly goes solo**,
because if the load comes up wrong nobody can tell whether it was the DLL or the
three def changes beside it.
**6. What a FALSE PASS looks like** — the way this particular check lies.

```
PROVE    <exact call / defName / click path>
EXPECT   <number or string, written before the look>
LIES     <how this check produces a false pass>
```

Three lines: the call, the expected reading, and how a pass could be false. 🔴 And first
ask whether it needs the game at all — the default is source. Rule and false-pass catalogue:
`skills/rimworld-modding/references/validation-plan.md`.

### The four ways a DEPLOY produces a false pass

1. **A successful write says nothing about the running game.** RimWorld parses defs
   and loads assemblies **once, at startup**. `--apply` reporting every file copied
   and verified is a statement about the filesystem; the process that matters read
   its copy minutes or hours ago. ⇒ **LIES** must name what the game last loaded
   and when, not what the plan printed.
2. **An assembly the game holds cannot be overwritten — and the failure is easy to
   file and forget.** Windows refuses with `WinError 1224` (§7), so the copy does
   not silently succeed; but the game folder is now carrying a **different build**
   from the repo, and nothing in the plan output distinguishes "same DLL" from
   "yesterday's DLL". **md5 both copies — it is the only way to know:**
   ```bash
   md5sum src/<Mod>/Assemblies/<Name>.dll "/mnt/c/Program Files (x86)/Steam/steamapps/common/RimWorld/Mods/<Mod>/Assemblies/<Name>.dll"
   ```
3. **An unscoped `--apply` deployed more than you think.** Five seats share one
   working tree, so a bare `--apply` sweeps up whatever else is dirty — including
   another seat's half-finished work — and any breakage in that load gets
   attributed to your change. ⇒ **Scope every deploy: `--mod <ModName>`**, and say
   in the plan which mods moved.
4. **"Deployed" and "live" are different words.** A folder under `Mods/` changes
   nothing until it is **enabled in the load order** (and, for a compatibility
   patch, enabled LAST — §8). The plan warns when a mod is absent from
   `ModsConfig.xml`; a plan that was not read is a mod that is on disk and inert.

### Worked example

A Harmony patch shipped as a new DLL for `Jawa_Patches`, deployed in the shutdown
window:

```
PROVE    Spawn Jawa + MeleeWeapon_Vibroblade, spawn a muffalo, draft and attack; watch the combat log
EXPECT   A Jawa with a vibroblade attacks twice in the time a vanilla knife pawn attacks once · Cooldown 1.4s (was 2.6s); Player.log prints "[Jawa_Patches] 3 patches applied"
LIES     Game copy may be the PREVIOUS build if RimWorld was running at deploy (WinError 1224); md5 both DLLs before the load. Absent Harmony line = patch never applied, not "nothing to report".
```

⚠️ **Write it in the same commit as the deploy.** The alternative is that whoever
holds the game invents a check, and theirs will not carry your prediction — which
is the field that turns a look into evidence.

## The deployed companion DLL runs behind source, and a missing tool is ambiguous

A companion assembly deploys only in a game-down window, so the game copy drifts behind the
repo for as long as the game stays up. Measured once at **166 tool names deployed against
238 built** — 670 KB of IL, everything written that day.

⇒ **A tool missing from `--list-tools` proves nothing on its own:** undeployed, gated out of
the build, or genuinely absent all read identically. Disambiguate with `build.py`'s own
`tool_surface()` over both DLLs.

⚠️ **That is a BYTE SCAN.** Its "added" list is untrustworthy — encoding differences make
tools that shipped weeks ago look new. Trust it for `LOST` being empty and for a name being
PRESENT; corroborate a gap with file size and the build commit stamped in the assembly.

⛔ **A `jawa/` literal written in PROSE inside a tool description becomes a phantom tool
name**, which makes `build.py`'s "THIS DEPLOY WOULD REMOVE TOOLS" guard lie in both
directions. After any description edit: `[x for x in surface if x.endswith('_')]`.

# HugeThings: owner answers (by question card, Wed 2026-11-11 12:16 AM PST)

Answers to QUESTIONS.md drafts 01, 02 and 04.

1. **What the promise leads with (01):** Two promises. Giant plants and titans are two different experiences; split the root into two promises, each with its own demonstration.
2. **First demonstration (02):** B, the titan's destructive crossing, then its death and the crowd that comes for the remains.
3. **Tremor warning (04):** written in: *"Two hours."* The warning before a titan arrives is two in-game hours (replacing the provisional six).

Drafts 03, 05 and 08 were asked on the second card below.

## Second card (Wed 2026-11-11 12:2x AM PST): drafts 03, 05, 08

4. **Root across a doorway (03):** written in: *"To be honest I don't really like the safety rule. I think they have to cut it down to get in or out after it grows."* The built door/access protection that keeps a cell open goes; a trunk that grows across a doorway seals it, and colonists cut the fungus down to get in or out.
5. **Fenced-out carcass visitors (05):** written in: *"Any of these depending on the faction. Faction dominates. Attack, negotiate, threaten, complain or just hover nearby and wait and sneak."* The response is chosen by the visiting faction's nature, from attack, negotiate, threaten, complain, or loiter and sneak in.
6. **Warned approach walled off (08):** Same side, it breaks through. The titan keeps its warned edge and tests the barrier under its normal wall/rock rules; thick rock may still hold.

Drafts 06–07 are not yet asked. Draft "Promise" above has changed draft 05's assumption that a single dispute rule exists: faction behaviour is the design.

## Third card (Wed 2026-11-11 12:35 AM PST): drafts 06, 07

7. **Prior claim on an older carcass (06):** Faction decides, visibly. As with the fence, the claim depends on the faction (a whole site, a sold share, or a fight), and it is visible before the colony's first harvest order.
8. **A serious harvest day (07):** Expedition, plenty left. Several colonists work the carcass at once with useful jobs (cutting, hauling), recovering enough to reward the trip, with plenty left for the next day and for competitors; tested with a small and a large colony.

All eight drafts are answered.
DRY RUN — HugeThings, proposed root and question bank. All wording and guesses below are mine, not Mandrake's words. Nothing is approved or sent.

This mod bundles several built promises: huge plants, huge animals, titan movement and damage, and the aftermath of a titan's death. Each needs its own proof.

PROPOSED ROOT

HugeThings makes huge plants and animals behave like the size you see: mass has consequences. A giant fungus has a solid stem and roots, open space beneath its cap, and a picture you can actually click; growing trunks respect the colony already around them. A huge animal has a body you can select, and a titan meets gaps, walls, roofs and trenches as a creature of its breadth: squeezing where it fits, breaking what it can, and being held by what really stops it. Its passage can wreck the colony simply because something that large walked through. A biome's own giants announce their approach with tremors. The largest dead titan becomes a landmark worked over days, with ordinary meat's rules for rot, while scavengers and visiting people compete for what remains. These are several connected promises, each owed its own demonstration. HugeThings supplies the common machinery; the biomes supply the living things, Large Pawns supplies their larger occupied bodies when loaded, and the plant and animal settings let the player tune their consequences.

My claim: making the visible size true is the common idea that joins these features.
The strongest objection: that paragraph can sound as if every part already works. Some parts are built but unaccepted; normal corpse rot and a real dispute over remains still have gaps. This is a proposed promise, not a report of passing tests.

These are eight drafts to choose from, not an eight-question interrogation. I would begin with 01–02, then serve at most three at a time as your answers make the later ones useful. A short phrase, a different scene, or “this doesn't matter to me” is enough. No reply is being assumed. I recommend the crossing-and-aftermath scene first because you already explained how its two actions belong together.

01. What the paragraph has to get right

Picture to react to (written thought experiment, not a capture or staged game): A colony lives among fungi whose trunks really take up ground. Later a titan crosses its outskirts, leaves damage, and eventually leaves remains worth going out to work.

Question: Which moment in that picture makes this HugeThings to you, and which sentence in the proposed root misstates what you expect?

Why it matters: F1/F2. 'Mass has consequences' could mean physical truth throughout play or mainly a dramatic titan story. The root must say the right thing without erasing either built half.

My guess, not your answer: Physical truth is the foundation; titan damage and the harvest race are the story it produces. I would lead with that.

What changes in the tree: If physical truth leads, the root and first explanatory examples centre on visible size matching interaction. If the story leads, reorder the root around passage and aftermath while retaining plant, selection and other built coverage. A correction changes dependent claims; no answer means no approved root.

02. The first demonstration

Picture to react to (written thought experiment, not a capture or staged game): Three labelled scene drafts: A, a working forest colony with solid trunks, open caps, clicks and growth; B, your destructive crossing followed by a force-kill and the rush to the remains; C, your older carcass already occupied by locals. These are descriptions, not staged or accepted scenes.

Question: Which scene would you put first when deciding whether HugeThings has understood you, and what single failure there would make you stop the demonstration?

Why it matters: F1/F2. Your two titan scenes are already valid; their order and the mod's flagship have not been picked in the evidence I found.

My guess, not your answer: B: the crossing makes the death and gathering crowds an understandable consequence. I recommend it first, with the forest as a separate demonstration.

What changes in the tree: The chosen scene becomes showcase 1 only after his recorded pick. The others remain candidates or ordinary scenes, with separate feature acceptance and an interaction scene. Root approval alone will not be stored as a flagship pick.

03. A root that must leave a doorway open

Picture to react to (written thought experiment, not a capture or staged game): A fungus grows beside a workshop. Its picture now puts a root across the doorway, but the safety rules leave that cell open rather than seal the workshop. Nothing is destroyed and nobody is moved.

Question: When you notice a colonist walking through that drawn root, what explanation or visible clue would make this exception make sense to you?

Why it matters: F1/F3. 'Solid where it touches ground' meets the already-built protection of doors and access. The mechanism is readable from code; the acceptable player explanation is not settled there.

My guess, not your answer: Safety wins, but clicking the fungus should explain that its trunk cannot fill the doorway. I would start with that small explanation rather than another warning letter.

What changes in the tree: If the explanation is essential, add an inspect/readability requirement tied to an actually refused cell and an obstruction/free-space control. If the exception needs no explanation, add no cue requirement and state the bounded solidity promise clearly. If the art itself must change, return to a labelled exploration before binding a visual leaf.

04. What the warning lets you do

Picture to react to (written thought experiment, not a capture or staged game): You get tremors from the east while colonists are working outside. The titan has not arrived. The current warning lasts six in-game hours; that number is a provisional setting.

Question: When it appears, which preparations should be finished, and which dangers should still surprise you?

Why it matters: F2. A delay and screen shake can satisfy 'warning' while giving the player no useful choice. Direction, identity, route certainty and available preparation time change that promise.

My guess, not your answer: Recall exposed workers and livestock and decide whether to get out of its way; no promise that a thin wall protects the base. I would preserve uncertainty about its exact route.

What changes in the tree: A recall window gives a scene with dispersed workers and a measured chance to shelter. A construction window requires a longer preparation case. Exact route knowledge would require honest route information and rewarning when it changes. His answer sets the experience bar, not an invented fixed number today.

05. The moment competitors become enemies

Picture to react to (written thought experiment, not a capture or staged game): People have arrived to feed from the remains. Your colonists build a fence that denies them access. Nobody has attacked anybody. In the current build they are ordinary non-hostile visitors; there is no carcass-specific dispute rule.

Question: What should those people do first, and what act by the colony would make a fight over the carcass deserved?

Why it matters: F2. 'The locals aren't too happy' does not yet say whether a fence means protest, trespass, negotiation or violence. The event's agent summary cannot decide that as your words.

My guess, not your answer: They object, then try to reach the food; the colony gets a readable chance to relent before deliberate exclusion becomes conflict. I would not make a first fence an instant silent war.

What changes in the tree: Protest/ultimatum needs a visible dispute state and a control where access is restored. Forced access needs behaviour around the fence. Negotiation needs a defined bargain. Violence needs an exact trigger, scope and stop condition. If ordinary visitor behaviour is enough, no new custom-hostility leaf is inferred.

06. What a prior claim means

Picture to react to (written thought experiment, not a capture or staged game): Your arriving clan finds the older carcass you described, with people already working beside it. A colonist walks up to work at the opposite side without attacking anyone.

Question: What do the people already there regard as theirs, and what could your clan do to earn a share?

Why it matters: F2. Prior presence can mean territorial ownership, a claimed portion, or simply rivals who resent sharing. Each gives the newcomer a different first decision.

My guess, not your answer: A prior group has a recognisable claim the newcomer must respect, buy into or challenge. I would make the claim visible before the first harvest order can offend them.

What changes in the tree: A whole-site claim needs ownership and permission; a portion needs separate accounted shares; open competition needs no title system, only rivalry. A bargain adds only the specific exchange he describes. The old carcass remains a hand-staged exploration/acceptance fixture until separate authority exists for spawning it in play.

07. A carcass worth rearranging the day for

Picture to react to (written thought experiment, not a capture or staged game): A large corpse lies outside a forty-colonist settlement. The current site permits one worker at a time, with a default hour of Mining work for a small batch. Rot must obey your ordinary-meat ruling; we cannot create urgency by making it rot faster.

Question: You decide to make a serious effort to recover it: what does that day's work look like, and what is left when the colony goes home?

Why it matters: F2/F3. 'Worked over days' can hide an idle queue behind one worker; an army harvesting instantly can erase the race. The intended commitment is not specified by the current batch sizes.

My guess, not your answer: A meaningful expedition with several useful jobs, enough recovery to reward choosing it, and plenty left for tomorrow and the competitors. I would test both a modest colony and a strong mobilisation.

What changes in the tree: Parallel work requires reservations/concurrency and pool-conservation acceptance. One specialist with supporting hauling instead needs useful throughput and support jobs demonstrated. The amount recovered and arrival pressure are tuned from his picture, with ordinary-temperature and frozen controls; no new artificial spoilage clock.

08. You change the way in after the tremors

Picture to react to (written thought experiment, not a capture or staged game): You hear tremors from the east, then finish a barrier across the warned entry. The current event checks the route again and may find a different entry or let the tremors fade. The new entry can be on another side of the colony.

Question: What should happen in the story when that approach becomes blocked, and what must the colony be told before danger comes from somewhere else?

Why it matters: F1/F2. An east warning followed by a west arrival can make preparation pointless; making every barrier cancel a titan can make mass meaningless. Built revalidation has not settled the desired play.

My guess, not your answer: It obeys its existing wall/rock rules, and a changed approach gives me a fresh honest warning. I would not silently swap edges at arrival time.

What changes in the tree: Same-edge persistence needs a real blocked-route clearing test. Another edge needs changed-direction communication and a defined preparation window. A justified retreat needs a reason the player can read. Thick rock and curated protections stay intact under every answer.

The underlying evidence and the built/proven/scope distinctions are in record.json. No capability is being offered for removal. These drafts have had a local evidence/wording check only; the role's fresh-agent review has not run.
One candidate question about a carcass that cannot fit beside a wall was excluded: earlier corpse-policy card answers need to be recovered before that subject is raised again.
DRY RUN — HugeThings Designer, stages 0 and 1 only

All three deliverables are agent-authored. The proposed root is in `root_draft`; `root` is null. The eight asks are `draft`, with independent review pending. There are no stand-in answers, owner approvals, waivers, stage results, build items or ledger writes. The source mirror was only read. Existing files in this working folder were left alone.

What this reading establishes

- HugeThings already contains both the plant engine and the merged titan engine. The inventory separates implementation, proof and scope for each capability, including supporting tooling, harness races, crown measurements and the GelatinousSlime boundary. `built_reviewed` maps source files, requested live/closed item prose, ledger-only work and live-proof pointers to those capabilities. Mapping a file is capability accounting, not a full-file code-review certificate.
- Several item files still describe pre-fix source and carry old NEXT lines. Current source already has settings sanitization, single-step wake deduplication, airborne suppression, maximum-life-stage qualification, roof route exclusion, clearing, atomic Large Pawns reconciliation, corpse conversion safety and test-honesty fixes. Those must not be offered as unbuilt features simply because their old item prose remains.
- The old Titanoslime spec is internally historical: its header says nothing is built and much early prose describes shrinking, while later sections and item results record a built creature and permanent growth by default. GelatinousSlime owns that mechanic and its registration fix. HugeThings consumes its size. No question reopens permanent growth, the lethal digestion, stage names or prey rule.
- Passage pool ownership changed after the original titan card. The current source follows biome hints and land/sea matching. Old item/script language about foreign creatures and recorded October outputs cannot be used as today's oracle. Sleeping Ice has explicit opt-outs; the Chill and Umbra decisions are feasibility/content work, not proof that new passage-sized residents have been built.

Important gaps, with no new decision invented

1. Ordinary meat rot is already ruled: `OWNER:1793738707492209767`. `Building_TitanicCorpseSite.ApplyDailySpoilage` still removes a flat fraction daily. The root proposes the ruled behaviour; it does not report it as implemented. No question asks him to approve normal rot again.
2. `ThickRoofCostProbe` reads a step cost. Its runner's `thick_roof_route_excluded` label overstates that observation. Route choice, footprint-edge clipping and escape need their own discriminating paths. A large cost or attached patch cannot substitute.
3. With `WallsSlotsActive`, the wake deliberately skips walls and doors. `RoofWallProbe` moves a pawn by assigning `Position`, without the path request that starts wall clearing. That is a concrete offline explanation to test for the intact-wall finding; it is not a proven live diagnosis or permission to weaken the wall promise.
4. The latest test-race A2 verification is 2026-11-06 at `7de03978ea8b`. Its contract permits exit 0 when each row is PASS **or a classified MOD FAIL**. The raw `/home/mandrake/rm/relentless/live/...` log is not in this mirror. I have not converted that event into all-mechanics-PASS.
5. Corpse creation, a forced visitor daily step and debug arrival are different observations from repeated harvest jobs, spontaneous visitor arrival, useful warning time or a satisfying race for resources. The owner rejected the combined November 3 demonstration. Historical October successes remain historical evidence.
6. A failed clear-4x4 conversion leaves an ordinary corpse and never retries. That can conflict with the worked-over-days promise. A candidate recovery question was excluded. The old review item says eight policy questions were ruled, but their complete card answers/full triage are not present in the supplied mirror files; independent review must check those original answers before drafting any potentially overlapping corpse-policy ask. This is an evidence-recovery task, not a reason to ask him to recall an old answer.

No gameplay or acceptance was run

I did not build, deploy, connect to the bridge, change ModsConfig, launch RimWorld, stage a scene, touch a save, run a live proof, validate art, bind an oracle, run an exam, file items or mark a first-touch pass. This was the requested reading and dialogue rehearsal. No proof is labelled `current`: I did not match the running build, settings, art and data fingerprints. `missing` means adequate acceptance evidence was not located here; it does not mean he never exercised the feature. I did not install anything or search for another runtime just to execute source tooling outside the requested dry run. The mirror has no `.git`; its `MIRROR_HEAD` was recorded in record.json. - `built_evidence` normally uses the ledger model's replay and the initialized alias list. I read the frozen ledger and matching shard events, plus the requested broader HUGE/TITAN item families and direct neighbours. I did not claim an official folded done-set or a successful Stage 0 check. A real launch should regenerate its exact required references and compare them with `built_reviewed` before accepting Stage 0.
- The role requires a fresh author-independent reviewer before questions reach him. This run has only a local evidence/wording check. There is no invented reviewer, `pass` verdict or token charge. The questions remain drafts for that review; they are not a protocol-approved sent turn.
- Eight questions are a bank, not one dialogue turn. The packet allows at most three at a time. Start with the root and flagship, then use the answers to prune the rest. Nothing changes on silence. The questions solicit a promise, concrete rejection cases and scenes; guesses are never stored as answers.
- The pictures in QUESTIONS.md are labelled written thought experiments. No live capture or visual mock was made. If question 03 leads to a choice about how a cue actually looks, show a labelled mock before binding that appearance. A prose explanation is not visual acceptance.
- The normal root field requires the owner's approval source. This dry run therefore uses null `root` and a separate agent `root_draft`, rather than putting proposed words under `speaker: owner`.
